The Referral Conversion Rate (C_ref) serves as a foundational sovereign primitive for quantifying the causal impact of peer-to-peer incentives on user acquisition and retention. Its mathematical structure mirrors that of a conditional probability, P(Target | Invitation), but it is distinguished by its operational focus on closed-loop system performance. In the GSI context, C_ref becomes a latent variable in hierarchical Bayesian models, allowing for shrinkage estimation across different referral channels and cohorts. The primary failure mode arises from contamination bias: if the invitation and control groups differ systematically on unobserved confounders (e.g., pre-existing interest), the estimated uplift will be spurious. To mitigate this, the epistemic trace advocates for randomized controlled trials (A/B tests) where the assignment to receive a referral link is independent of user characteristics. Additionally, the primitive must be robustified against winner's curse effects, where early adopters artificially inflate observed rates due to their inherent stickiness. The derived kernel in GSE situational reasoning involves integrating C_ref into Markov decision processes, optimizing sequential referral outreach policies that balance exploration (testing new incentivization structures) and exploitation (scaling high-performing ones).
